newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ferre bids Dior farewell, Galliano tipped for job.
newsitem.headline: Ferre bids Dior farewell, Galliano tipped for job.

text.p: Italian designer Gianfranco Ferre bade an emotional farewell to Paris on Tuesday, sending out his last collection for Christian Dior amid whispers that Britain's John Galliano will take over at the legendary fashion house.
Ferre, hired at Dior in 1989, told a crush of cameramen and photographers after the show: "A page has turned. It's eight years of my life. I feel serene."

The collection, a medley of skin-tight drainpipe trousers with bustier tops, bauble-encrusted cocktail shifts and black and white candy-striped beach-wear, was an upbeat last hurrah from Ferre before he returns to Milan to devote himself to his own prospering fashion house.

There were black babydoll cocktail numbers, backless evening sheaths in brilliant shades and a finale of slim white chiffon evening gowns with heightened waists and lilies dangling from the shoulders.

"I think he did an extraordinary job for Dior and it was a beautiful good-bye," said Nicole Fischelis of Saks Fifth Avenue department store. "He handled his last collection with great style and great beauty."

For much of the British and French media, the appointment of Galliano as Ferre's successor is a foregone conclusion. But the fashion community will have to wait until October 15 for the official announcement.

If it turns out to be true, Galliano's job will be open at Givenchy, where in barely a year the 36-year-old designer has turned the label's prim and proper styles into some of the most wild, sexy and theatrical clothes around.
Both houses belong to luxury goods giant LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton whose chairman Bernard Arnault has been methodically gathering the young, creative lifeblood of fashion into his empire.

Some press reports say that Arnault offered the Dior position to Christian Lacroix, another member of the LVMH pack, but the flamboyant, iconoclastic designer turned it down, determined to focus on his own line.
The succession question is the biggest news of the season and the choices will be a high-risk gamble.

Both the Dior and Givenchy jobs are formidable, demanding the creation of at least four collections per year -- two haute couture and two ready-to-wear -- and the responsibilty for brand images that sell hundreds of millions of dollars worth of perfumes, watches, scarfs and panty hose.
Alexander McQueen, a subversive 27-year-old Briton, is tipped for the job of keeping the prestigious, 40-year-old Givenchy label on fashion's sharpest edge if Galliano leaves.
The big question fashion watchers are asking is: would McQueen, who fancies blood stains -- real -- human hair and insects to decorate his creations, be up to the job?
He told the trade paper Women's Wear Daily last month: "They haven't made up their minds and neither have I."
